newsitem.title: USA: Earnings joy seen over for Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Earnings joy seen over for Wall Street.

text.p: Wall Street has got about as much of a boost as it will get from the first quarter's better-than-expected corporate earnings.
The strong results stemmed a month-long slide by U.S. stocks but with three-quarters of the reports out, the good news has already been accounted for, analysts said.

While they expect the balance of the reports to generally reflect the trend, they said the stock market is bound to turn its attention away from earnings and toward the threat of rising interest rates.
"The tail of these earnings will probably not have a very significant effect," said Robert Robbins, market strategist at Robinson-Humphrey Co.

Of the 78 percent of Standard & Poor's 500 companies having reported through Friday, 61 percent posted results that beat Wall Street expectations, said Joseph Abbott, assistant vice president at I/B/E/S, which tracks analysts forecasts.
Earnings for the S&P 500 companies will likely show a 15 percent rise over 1996's first quarter, said Chuck Hill, director of research at estimate-tracking firm First Call.
Expectations at the outset of the reporting period were for a 12 percent rise, he said.
The Dow industrials lost about 700 points in a slide that began March 12 and hit its low point on April 11. The strong earnings led to a rebound in which the Dow recouped more than 400 points.
Late last week, however, there was evidence the earnings-driven rebound was losing steam.

Better-than-expected earnings from International Business Machines Corp. late Wednesday shot the Dow up almost 80 points early Thursday. But the rally fizzled and the Dow ended that day down 20 points.
On Friday the Dow fell 53 points to 6,739. For the week, the Dow gained 35.32 points.
A slew of economic data this week, including the first-quarter Employment Cost Index on Tuesday and April jobs data on Friday, will likely overshadow any corporate reports yet to come.
Some insurance firms and retailers are among the groups yet to post first quarter numbers.

Analysts said the robust earnings, while giving a short-term lift to the stock market, also serve as further evidence of a strong economy. The prospects that the Federal Reserve will have to further raise interest rates to cool the economy could put stocks back on the ropes, analysts said.
"We're having a pretty strong quarter" in terms of earnings, Abbott said. "The only problem is, when you have growth, you also have to watch out for interest rates."
Despite the rally, the market has not been overly generous to companies posting surprisingly good results.

Paul Rabbitt, quantitative analyst at Oppenheimer & Co., said that over the past 90 days, the companies in the Russell 3000 index posting the top earnings surprises saw their stocks drop on average 8.7 percent. While those posting the biggest earnings disappointments fell 2 percent, he daid.
"The nature of a bear market is when people sell good stocks on good news," Rabbitt said.
